pages.title: Bash basics
pages.summary: Commands, paths, wildcards, quoting, variables, exit status, pipes and redirection.

sections.title: What the shell is
body: A shell is a program that reads what you type, runs it, and shows you the result. Bash is the most common one on Linux and the default on many other systems. You type a line at the prompt, press Enter, and the shell finds the program or built-in command you named and runs it.

Everything on this site that shows a result was run in a real Bash 5.2 shell, in a sandbox folder with a few sample files, so the output you see is what Bash printed. Paths are shown as /home/you/demo.

sections.title: Anatomy of a command
body: A command line is words separated by spaces. The first word is the command; the rest are options (usually starting with a dash) and arguments (what to act on). The shell splits the line into words before running anything, which is why spaces matter so much.
Options can often be combined: ls -l -a and ls -la mean the same thing. Long options start with two dashes, such as --help.

blocks.note: Extra spaces vanish: the shell passes three separate words to echo.
Here -l asks for the long format; cut keeps the first ten characters, the permissions.

sections.title: Where am I? Paths
body: The shell is always 'in' a directory. pwd prints it, cd moves it. A path that starts with / is absolute and begins at the root of the file system. Any other path is relative to where you are. A single dot (.) means here and two dots (..) mean the parent. A tilde (~) means your home directory.
Hidden files are ordinary files whose names start with a dot; ls leaves them out unless you add -a.

blocks.note: A relative path that goes up one level and down again.
An absolute path works from anywhere.

sections.title: Wildcards
body: Before running a command, the shell expands patterns in file names: * matches any run of characters (including none), ? matches exactly one character, and [abc] matches one character from the set. This is called globbing, and the command only ever sees the expanded list.
If nothing matches, Bash passes the pattern through unchanged, which is why a typo can look like a missing file.

blocks.note: No match, so the pattern comes back as typed.

sections.title: Quoting
body: Quotes tell the shell how much to interpret. Double quotes keep spaces together but still expand variables. Single quotes keep everything exactly as typed. A backslash escapes one character. Leaving quotes off lets the shell split a value at its spaces, a common cause of bugs with file names that contain spaces.
The rule that prevents most mistakes: put double quotes around every variable you expand, such as "$name".

blocks.code:
name="Ana Lee"
echo "Hello, $name"
echo 'Hello, $name'
echo Hello, \$name

blocks.note: Without quotes the value is split into two words; with quotes it stays one.

sections.title: Variables and the environment
body: Assign with NAME=value, with no spaces around the equals sign, and read with $NAME. Variables belong to the current shell only. export marks a variable so programs started from this shell inherit it; those programs are what other tools call the environment. PATH is the best-known one: a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches for programs.
Command substitution, $(command), puts a command's output where it appears.

blocks.code:
COLOR=blue
bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$COLOR]"'
export COLOR
bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$COLOR]"'
blocks.note: Only the exported variable reaches the child shell.

sections.title: Exit status and chaining
body: Every command ends with a number: 0 means success and anything else means failure. $? holds the last one. The shell uses it to chain commands: A && B runs B only if A succeeded, A || B runs B only if A failed, and A ; B runs both regardless.
This is also what makes if statements work in scripts: they test a command's exit status, not its output.

blocks.note: The first line is the error message, from ls itself.

sections.title: Pipes and redirection
body: Programs read from standard input and write to standard output and standard error. A pipe (|) connects one program's output to the next one's input, so small tools combine into larger ones. Redirection sends a stream to a file instead: > overwrites, >> appends, < reads from a file, and 2> redirects error messages.
Careful: > truncates the file the moment the command starts, before anything is written. A typo there can empty a file you meant to read.

blocks.code:
echo hi > out.txt
echo again >> out.txt
cat out.txt

sections.title: Getting help
body: Three places answer most questions. man NAME opens the manual page (press q to leave). NAME --help prints a short summary for most programs. type NAME tells you whether a word is a built-in, an alias, a function or a program, and help NAME documents the built-ins.
Manual pages describe your system's version of a tool. GNU (Linux) and BSD (macOS) versions of the same command differ in some flags; the command reference notes where.

blocks.note: builtin, file (a program on disk), keyword.
GNU ls. On macOS use man ls, because BSD ls has no --help.

pages.title: Scripting
pages.summary: Write scripts that take arguments, decide, loop, define functions and fail safely.

sections.title: A first script
body: A script is a text file of commands. The first line, the shebang, names the interpreter. #!/usr/bin/env bash finds bash on your PATH, which is more portable than hard-coding /bin/bash. Make the file executable with chmod +x and run it with a path, because the current directory is not on PATH.
Arguments arrive as $1, $2 and so on; $0 is the script's name, $# the number of arguments and "$@" all of them, each kept as one word.

blocks.code:
cat > hello.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
name=${1:-world}
echo "Hello, $name! ($# argument(s))"
EOF
chmod +x hello.sh
./hello.sh
./hello.sh Ana
blocks.note: ${1:-world} means: the first argument, or the word world if there is none.

blocks.code:
cat > args.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for a in "$@"; do echo "arg: [$a]"; done
EOF
bash args.sh one 'two words' three

sections.title: Making decisions
body: if runs a command and branches on its exit status. The usual command is a test: [[ ... ]] in Bash (a keyword, safer with spaces and empty values) or [ ... ] in any POSIX shell. Compare numbers with -eq, -lt, -gt and strings with == and !=. File tests include -f (a regular file), -d (a directory) and -e (exists).
case matches a value against patterns and is tidier than a long if chain.

blocks.code:
n=7
if [[ $n -gt 5 ]]; then echo big; else echo small; fi

for f in notes.txt nothere.txt docs; do
  if [[ -f $f ]]; then echo "$f: file"
  elif [[ -d $f ]]; then echo "$f: directory"
  else echo "$f: missing"; fi
done

sections.title: Loops
body: for repeats over a list, which is often a glob. while repeats while a command succeeds; with read it processes a file line by line. break leaves a loop and continue skips to the next round.
Use read -r so backslashes in the data are not treated as escapes, and IFS= to keep leading spaces.

blocks.code: for f in *.txt; do echo "$f has $(wc -l < "$f") lines"; done
for ((i = 1; i <= 3; i++)); do echo "round $i"; done
while IFS= read -r line; do echo "> $line"; done < fruits.txt | head -n 3

for n in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  [[ $n -eq 2 ]] && continue
  [[ $n -eq 4 ]] && break
  echo $n
done

sections.title: Functions
body: A function groups commands under a name. Its arguments are $1, $2, ... inside it. Declare variables with local so they do not leak. A function can return a status with return (0 to 255), but it hands back text by printing it, which the caller captures with $(...).
Define functions before you call them.

blocks.note: The arithmetic test's own exit status becomes the function's status.

sections.title: Parameter expansion
body: Bash can edit a variable's value as it expands it, with no external programs. ${var:-default} supplies a default, ${#var} gives the length, ${var#pattern} and ${var##pattern} remove a prefix (shortest and longest match), ${var%pattern} and ${var%%pattern} remove a suffix, and ${var/old/new} substitutes.
These are quicker and safer than calling sed or basename for simple edits.

blocks.note: The same results as basename and dirname, without starting a program.

sections.title: Arrays
body: An indexed array holds several values: items=(a b c). Read one with ${items[0]}, all of them with "${items[@]}" (quoted, so each stays one word), and the count with ${#items[@]}. Associative arrays (declare -A) map names to values but need Bash 4 or newer; macOS still ships Bash 3.2, which has neither the feature nor several others used on this site.

blocks.code:
items=(apple 'sweet pear' cherry)
echo "first: ${items[0]}"
echo "count: ${#items[@]}"
for i in "${items[@]}"; do echo "- $i"; done

declare -A age
age[ana]=31
age[ben]=27
echo "ana is ${age[ana]}"
blocks.note: Needs Bash 4 or newer.

sections.title: Failing safely
body: By default a script carries on after an error. Three settings change that: set -e exits when a command fails, set -u treats an unset variable as an error, and set -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails (otherwise only the last stage counts). Together, set -euo pipefail at the top is a common safety net.
It is not a cure-all: set -e ignores failures inside if conditions and && lists, and it can surprise you. Check the cases you care about explicitly, and run ShellCheck over your scripts.

blocks.code: bash -c 'set -e; false; echo "never printed"'; echo "exit status: $?"

bash -c 'false | true; echo "without pipefail: $?"'
bash -c 'set -o pipefail; false | true; echo "with pipefail: $?"'

blocks.note: A typo in a variable name (dirr) is caught instead of silently expanding to nothing. Without set -u that command would read rm -rf /.

sections.title: A worked example: which pages are missing?
body: Log files record one event per line, and a pipeline of small tools answers questions about them without a database. The sample log in this sandbox has 40 requests. Which pages returned status 404 (not found), and how often?
Each stage does one job: awk keeps the path of lines whose ninth field is 404, sort groups equal paths together, uniq -c counts each group, and sort -rn puts the biggest count first.

blocks.note: ${1:?message} stops the script with a usage message when the argument is missing.

sections.title: Safety habits
body: Quote your variables. Prefer set -euo pipefail while developing. Print a command before you run something destructive (echo rm ... first). Never run a script you have not read, especially a one-liner that pipes a download into a shell. Use mktemp for temporary files instead of fixed names. Keep secrets out of command lines, where other users can see them in the process list.
ShellCheck (shellcheck.net) catches many of these mistakes automatically and explains each warning.

blocks.note: Prefix a dangerous command with echo to see exactly what it would do.

blocks.code:
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
test -d "$tmp" && echo "temporary directory created"
rmdir "$tmp"

pages.title: Advanced topics
pages.summary: File descriptors, here-documents, process substitution, jobs, traps, debugging and portability.

sections.title: File descriptors and redirection
body: Every process has numbered streams: 0 is standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error. N> redirects stream N, and 2>&1 means 'send stream 2 to wherever stream 1 now goes'. Order matters: redirections are processed left to right.
&> file sends both streams to a file in Bash. /dev/null discards anything written to it.

blocks.code:
ls notes.txt nothere > both.txt 2>&1
cat both.txt
blocks.note: Both streams end up in the file.

blocks.code:
ls notes.txt nothere 2>&1 > only-out.txt
echo '--- file:'
cat only-out.txt
blocks.note: Reversed order: stderr was pointed at the terminal first, so the error is not in the file.

sections.title: Here-documents and here-strings
body: A here-document feeds several lines to a command: command <<'EOF' ... EOF. Quoting the delimiter ('EOF') stops the shell from expanding variables inside; leave it unquoted to expand them. A here-string, <<< word, feeds one string.
Use <<- with tab indentation to strip leading tabs.

blocks.code:
name=Ana
cat <<EOF
Hello, $name
Home is a variable here too.
EOF

read -r first rest <<< "alpha beta gamma"
echo "$first | $rest"

sections.title: Process substitution and command grouping
body: <(command) makes a command's output look like a file, so you can compare or join two results without temporary files. ( ... ) runs commands in a subshell, a copy of the shell whose changes (such as cd or variable assignments) are discarded afterwards. { ...; } groups commands in the current shell, handy for redirecting all their output at once.
Process substitution is a Bash feature; it is not part of POSIX sh.

blocks.note: Compares two commands' output as if they were files; no temporary file is needed.
The cd happened only inside the parentheses.

blocks.code:
{ echo one; echo two; } > pair.txt
cat pair.txt

sections.title: Brace expansion, arithmetic and substitution
body: Brace expansion builds lists before anything else happens: {a,b,c} and {1..5}. $(( expression )) does integer arithmetic (no decimals). $(command) captures output, and unlike the older backticks it nests.
Bash 4 added case conversion: ${var^^} for upper case and ${var,,} for lower.

blocks.note: Integer division: the fractional part is dropped.
Needs Bash 4 or newer.

sections.title: Background jobs
body: End a command with & to run it in the background. wait pauses until background jobs finish. $! holds the last background job's process ID. Interactive shells also offer jobs, fg and bg, and Ctrl-Z to suspend a program.
A background job still writes to your terminal and is stopped when the terminal closes, unless you use nohup or a terminal multiplexer.

blocks.code:
sleep 0.2 &
echo "started in the background"
wait
echo "finished"

(sleep 0.1; echo job A done) &
(sleep 0.2; echo job B done) &
wait
echo all done

sections.title: Cleaning up with trap
body: trap 'commands' SIGNAL runs commands when the shell receives a signal or an event. The EXIT pseudo-signal fires whenever the script ends, however it ends, which makes it the right place to delete temporary files. Traps for INT (Ctrl-C) and TERM let a script clean up when interrupted.

blocks.code:
trap 'echo cleaning up' EXIT
echo working
exit 3
blocks.note: The trap runs even though the script exits early.

sections.title: Debugging
body: bash -x script.sh, or set -x inside a script, prints each command after expansion, prefixed with +, so you can see exactly what Bash ran. bash -n script.sh checks syntax without running anything. ShellCheck finds quoting mistakes, unused variables and portability problems before you run the script.
Add a PS4 prefix with the line number for long scripts: PS4='+ line $LINENO: '.

blocks.code:
cat > bad.sh <<'EOF'
if true; then
  echo missing the closing fi
EOF
bash -n bad.sh; echo "syntax check status: $?"
blocks.note: Exit status 2 means a syntax error; nothing in the script ran.

sections.title: Bash versus POSIX sh, GNU versus BSD
body: Not every system is the same. #!/bin/sh may be a smaller shell (dash on Debian and Ubuntu) that lacks [[ ]], arrays, process substitution and more. macOS ships Bash 3.2 and BSD versions of tools: sed -i needs an argument (sed -i ''), date -d does not exist, and some grep and ls flags differ. If a script must run everywhere, write for POSIX sh and test with a strict shell; if it can require Bash, say so in the shebang and in the README.
The command reference marks GNU-only flags.

blocks.note: The Bash version used to produce every output on this site.
